title: De Morgan's Laws
short: ¬(p ∧ q) is equivalent to ¬p ∨ ¬q, and ¬(p ∨ q) to ¬p ∧ ¬q: moving a negation inside flips ∧ and ∨.
trouble: The scope of negation: learners distribute the ¬ but keep the same connective, writing ¬(p ∧ q) as ¬p ∧ ¬q.

blocks.html: Some equivalences (Logical Equivalence) come up so often that they have names. The most useful pair is De Morgan's laws, which tell you how to move a negation inside parentheses.

$
eg (p \land q)$ is equivalent to $
eg p \lor 
eg q$, and $
eg (p \lor q)$ is equivalent to $
eg p \land 
eg q$. When the negation moves inside, it goes onto each part and the connective switches.

"Not both" means at least one fails: $
eg (p \land q)$ is true when $p$ is false or $q$ is false, which is $
eg p \lor 
eg q$. "Not either" means neither holds: $
eg (p \lor q)$ is true only when $p$ is false and $q$ is false, which is $
eg p \land 
eg q$. In everyday words: it is not true that the bakery has both bread and muffins exactly when it lacks bread or lacks muffins.

blocks.title: Move the negation in
blocks.q: Rewrite $\neg (r \land s)$ without a $\neg$ in front of the parentheses.

blocks.title: Parts that are already negated
steps:
Negate each part: $
eg 
eg p$ and $
eg q$.
A double negation may be dropped: $\neg \neg p$ is equivalent to $p$.

blocks.title: Pull it out
blocks.q: Write $\neg p \lor \neg q$ as the negation of one formula.
steps: Read De Morgan right to left.
Take the negations off, switch $\lor$ to $\land$, and negate the whole.

blocks.html: Both laws come from one idea. A conjunction claims every part; to deny it you only need one part to fail, so the denial is a disjunction of failures. A disjunction claims at least one part; to deny it every part must fail, so the denial is a conjunction of failures. Once you see that, you will not need to memorize which way the connective switches.

blocks.title: In English
blocks.q: Rewrite "It is not the case that both the gate is open and the dog is outside" without "both".
blocks.a: "Either the gate is not open or the dog is not outside."

blocks.html:
Distributing the $
eg$ but keeping the connective: writing $
eg (p \land q)$ as $
eg p \land 
eg q$. Check the row $p$ T, $q$ F: $
eg (p \land q)$ is T, but $
eg p \land 
eg q$ is F. The connective must switch. A quick memory aid: the negation "flips" both the parts and the connective.

items: Negation over $\land$: negate each part, switch to $\lor$.
Negation over $\lor$: negate each part, switch to $\land$.
Cancel any double negation $\neg \neg p$ to $p$ if you like; they are equivalent.
Check one row with the truth table if you are unsure.

blocks.html:
The same laws work with larger parts: $
eg ((p 	o q) \lor r)$ becomes $
eg (p 	o q) \land 
eg r$. And they apply in English: "it is not the case that either the bus is late or the train is late" says the bus is not late and the train is not late.
